name: Panama
summary: There is no fixed share for children, but relatives have a right to maintenance that comes before the will's beneficiaries: children up to age 25, disabled children, parents and the spouse. Panama is the clearest trust-and-foundation jurisdiction here: it has a trust law (Law 1 of 1984), a private interest foundation law (Law 25 of 1995), and the Hague Trusts Convention is in force.
family_claims: Panamanian law gives certain relatives a right to maintenance (children up to 25, disabled children, parents, spouse) that takes precedence over beneficiaries named in a will (secondary source, no article cited).
foreign_law_note: Not sourced: Panama's private international law code (Law 61 of 2015) rule on the law applicable to succession was not read.
trust_note: Hague Trusts Convention: accession 30 Aug 2017, in force 1 Dec 2018 (HCCH table). Trust Law 1 of 1984, as amended by Law 21 of 2017, governs trusts; professional trustees need a licence from the Superintendency of Banks. Private Interest Foundations: Law 25 of 12 June 1995; art. 14 says heirship rules of the founder's or beneficiaries' domicile cannot be enforced against the foundation, but a foreign court applying its own law can still look through it.
open_questions: Civil Code articles on maintenance and any compulsory share were not read; the no-heirship finding rests on two secondary sources.
Law 61 of 2015 (private international law) was not read; foreign_law_choice is unclear.
Whether Panamanian courts would apply art. 14 of Law 25 against a Panamanian-domiciled founder's heirs was not sourced.
